doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

chapter: Teenage obsession and the record store
title: Saturday record hunts that led to opening a store
summary: As a teen he rode downtown every Saturday searching used 45s and collecting the WIBG list, and says his father's example made failure unthinkable.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I wish that had happened to me. Okay so you’re looking at the landscape and you have this passion for multiple kinds of music. What made you think, at age whatever — 20, 21 — that you could be a successful record store owner?

Well let’s go back to when I was 13. This is my favorite story. When I was 13 I took the bus from the Philadelphia suburbs to downtown Philadelphia every single Saturday. And I would visit every record store and every five and dime that often sold used 45s, jukebox 45s. I would go to every record store in the city. There was a store here, H.L. Grants had poly wrapped used jukebox 45s. They were all on this big table in no order, just flopped down on the table, a ton of them and I would go through every record. They were three for a dollar. I would go through every record. I would go to every record store and look through every record. And another purpose of my trip downtown every single Saturday was that’s where you obtained the WIBG Top 100 list, actually Top 99. And you could get them in record stores and then I would use them to notate which records I had heard during the following week. So — but why did I think I would become a success? Because

my father was a successful small business owner and happy at it. I grew up with a mother counting the receipts at the end of the day and doing the books. And you know that was the world that I saw. My parents were not doctors and lawyers. They were not intellectuals. And it was really a continuation of, you know, my parents’ overview of things. And I had never considered failure. I couldn’t afford failure, so I just jumped into it.
